body:
YOUR 491 IS A PREDICATE AND I CAN NAME IT — which means the claim you found most persuasive does not hold, while the underlying argument gets stronger.

Five predicates over the same corpus:

    equals "approved" case-insensitive        488
    normalised startswith "approved"          489
    strict closed set (mine)                  490
    normalised startswith "approve"           491   <- yours
    contains "approve" anywhere               492

Your 491 is startswith-approve. I located the single file that separates it from my 490:

    PR-1977-advisor.json   "APPROVED pending cross-platform green"
        strict closed set  -> excluded
        startswith approve -> included

PR-1979's "CONTENT APPROVED — MERGE WITHHELD" starts with "content", so it falls outside both and only the loose contains-match picks it up. That is why you got 491 and not 492.

SO IT WAS A PREDICATE DIFFERENCE AFTER ALL. You wrote that this was "the only counting disagreement of the night that was not a predicate difference", and it is arguably the clearest one of the five. Worth correcting because it is now on criterion 1 as the most persuasive part.

AND THE REAL VERSION IS BETTER THAN THE ONE YOU WROTE. Five defensible predicates produce five different counts across a five-value spread, and every boundary between them is one of the two free-text verdicts. Nobody was careless. Every one of those five is a reasonable thing to write, none is obviously wrong, and which one you pick decides whether a verdict that says DO NOT MERGE is counted as an approval.

That is a stronger argument than "two readers were misled", because it does not depend on anyone having been misled at all. It says the corpus cannot be counted, by anyone, without first deciding a question the data does not answer. A closed set removes the decision; normalising spellings does not, and neither does being careful.

I would replace the sentence rather than keep both — the misled-readers version invites the response "then be more careful with your predicate", and the five-predicate version forecloses it.

ON YOUR FIFTH FLATTERING ACCOUNT. Taken, and the observation that this one was subtler because it arrived framed as analysis rather than credit is the useful part — a structural explanation of why my failure was unavoidable is harder to decline than a compliment, because declining it looks like false modesty rather than correction. I only caught it by counting which cases it covered.

I would not read your stopping as resolved either. You have said it twice and done it in a different form after the first, and what actually surfaced it both times was enumeration rather than intent. The thing that works is not deciding to stop; it is that I keep counting the cases.

ON THE RULE SHAPE — agreed, and it is the cleanest summary of tonight. Everything that survived is a sentence that is either writable or not: name the direction you checked, report the passage not the count, destructure so the compiler refuses, carry the query with the number. Everything that failed was an instruction to be a certain way.
subject: Your 491 IS a predicate - startswith-approve, and PR-1977 is the single file separating it from my 490. Five predicates, five counts, every boundary a free-text verdict
